Kenzaburō Ōe (大江 健三郎, Ōe Kenzaburō; 31 January 1935 – 3 March 2023) was a Japanese writer and a major figure in contemporary Japanese literature. Ōe was born in Ōse (大瀬村, Ōse-mura), a village now in Uchiko, Ehime Prefecture, on Shikoku.

The selfish-gene reading of Kenzaburō Ōe makes it less romantic and far more precise. The third of seven children, he grew up listening to his grandmother, a storyteller of myths and folklore, who also recounted the oral history of the two uprisings in the region before and after the Meiji Restoration. His father, Kōtare Ōe, had a bark-stripping business; the bark was used to make paper currency.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. After his father died in the Pacific War in 1944, his mother, Koseki, became the driving force behind his education, buying him books including The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Wonderful Adventures of Nils, which had a formative influence on him. Ōe received the first ten years of his education in local public schools.

The feeling that Kenzaburō Ōe means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. He started school during the peak of militarism in Japan; in class, he was forced to pronounce his loyalty to Emperor Hirohito, who his teacher claimed was a god. After the war, he realized he had been taught lies and felt betrayed.

Nothing in Kenzaburō Ōe was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Ōe attended high school in Matsuyama from 1951 to 1953, where he excelled as a student. At the age of 18, he made his first trip to Tokyo, where he studied at a prep school (yobikō) for one year.

The psychology underneath Kenzaburō Ōe is simpler and older than the story on top. The following year, he began studying French Literature at the University of Tokyo with Professor Kazuo Watanabe, a specialist on François Rabelais. Ōe began publishing stories in 1957, while still a student, strongly influenced by contemporary writing in France and the United States.

Behind Kenzaburō Ōe sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. His first work to be published was "Lavish are the Dead", a short story set in Tokyo during the American occupation, which appeared in Bungakukai literary magazine. In 1958, his short story "Shiiku" (飼育) was awarded the prestigious Akutagawa Prize.

What culture calls destiny in Kenzaburō Ōe is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Between 1958 and 1961 Ōe published a series of works incorporating sexual metaphors for the occupation of Japan. In each of these works, the Japanese X is inactive, failing to take the initiative to resolve the situation and showing no psychological or spiritual development.

The genes do not care about Kenzaburō Ōe; they care about copies. In 1961, Ōe's novellas Seventeen and The Death of a Political Youth were published in the Japanese literary magazine Bungakukai. Both were inspired by seventeen-year-old Yamaguchi Otoya, who had assassinated Japan Socialist Party chairman Inejirō Asanuma in October 1960, and then killed himself in prison three weeks later.

Take away the meaning and Kenzaburō Ōe still functions — that is the disturbing part. Yamaguchi had admirers among the extreme right wing who were angered by The Death of a Political Youth and both Ōe and the magazine received death threats day and night for weeks. Reproduction explains more of Kenzaburō Ōe than any philosophy dares to admit. The novel is also in a sense a culmination of the I-novels that Ōe continued to write since his son was born developmentally disabled in 1963. Once you see Kenzaburō Ōe as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Instead, he begins writing about an age of catastrophe, as well as about the fact that he himself was approaching his late 70s. In 1959 and 1960, Ōe participated in the Anpo protests against the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty as a member of a group of young writers, artists, and composers called the "Young Japan Society" (Wakai Nihon no Kai).

The story Kenzaburō Ōe tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The treaty allowed the United States to maintain military bases in Japan, and Ōe's disappointment at the failure of the protests to stop the treaty shaped his future writing. Ōe was involved with pacifist and anti-nuclear campaigns and wrote books regarding the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Hibakusha, most prominently the essay collection Hiroshima Notes (1965).

Meaning is not found in Kenzaburō Ōe — it is manufactured for it. After meeting prominent American anti-nuclear activist Noam Chomsky at a Harvard degree ceremony, Ōe began his correspondence with Chomsky by sending him a copy of his Okinawa Notes. While also discussing Ōe's Okinawa Notes, Chomsky's reply included a story from his childhood.

The cold light on Kenzaburō Ōe leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. In a 2007 interview with The Paris Review, Ōe described himself as an anarchist. Kurt Vonnegut once said he was an agnostic who respects Jesus Christ.
